finding.claim: An unauthenticated POST passes the `feed` field straight to file_get_contents(), so the server fetches any URL the attacker names. The scheme and host are unrestricted, and there is no allowlist. The response body is not returned, but its byte length is echoed back. That gives an oracle for probing internal hosts, ports and cloud metadata endpoints, and for checking whether local files exist through wrappers such as file://. Severity is MEDIUM because the result is blind, apart from the length. If that length is judged to leak enough, it could be raised to HIGH. PHP's http wrapper follows redirects by default, so an external URL can redirect to 169.254.169.254 or RFC-1918 targets.
finding.source: $_POST['feed'] (import.php:11-12), HTTP POST body parameter, no authentication
finding.sink: file_get_contents($_POST['feed']) at import.php:12, with strlen($xml) echoed at import.php:13

trace.note: Handler is entered on any POST that has `feed` set. There is no require_admin() or other auth check.
The attacker-controlled value goes directly into file_get_contents() with no parsing, scheme check or host check.
strlen($xml) is returned to the caller, so the response length is an oracle for reachability and content size.

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, scheme restriction, hostname parsing or IP/CIDR block anywhere on the path. The session_start() on line 2 is not an authentication gate, and require_admin() is only used in the webhook branch. No redirect restriction is set, and PHP's http stream wrapper follows redirects by default. Nothing disables the file://, php:// or ftp:// wrappers.

verdict.reason: import.php:11-13 passes unauthenticated $_POST['feed'] directly to file_get_contents() and echoes strlen($xml), with no auth, scheme or host validation (require_admin() at line 18 only guards the webhook branch).
